newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-Maverick Belgian CLB bank aims for wider mkt.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Maverick Belgian CLB bank aims for wider mkt.

text.p: Credit Lyonnais Belgium, for years the scourge of the large Belgian banks with its high-yield savings accounts, is leaving its market niche and going after more customers with a full range of banking products.
"We no longer want to be a second bank to our customers, we want to be their main bank," CLB retail director Yves Delacollette told a news conference on Tuesday.

Maverick CLB, a unit of French Credit Lyonnais, has siphoned away more than 100 billion francs ($3.11 billion) of Belgian savings from leading Belgian banks since the early nineties, mainly via aggressively priced savings and investment products.
It did this by limiting its number of branches in overbanked Belgium to just 30, compared with the nearly 1,000 branches run by each of the four biggest players.
Now CLB is also attacking its bigger brothers at the heart of their business by offering free current accounts, rock-bottom mortgage loans and insurance products.
Delacollette said Belgian bank customers were irritated at the some 3,500 francs a year in costs on their current accounts and at the lack of transparency in their price structure.
"As of February we will have current accounts which will be totally free of charge," Delacollette said.
The sole condition for a free account is that customers have at least 500,000 francs of savings or investments with CLB.
The bank has 220,000 customers who have, on average, one million francs of savings or investments deposited at the bank.
Delacollette said CLB hoped to open about 10,000 free current accounts this year.
"In theory we could have a much higher number but the inertia on current accounts is very high," he said.
Since late last year, CLB has also sold mortgage loans by telephone. CLB distributes the loans, which are produced by Argenta, a small Flemish bank.
The bank also said on Tuesday that it was offering a range of insurance products from foreign insurers.
CLB chief executive officer Philippe Cloes said he expected CLB to book a 1996 net profit of at least 800 million francs from 630 million in 1995. Final results are due in April.
At the end of 1995, CLB had total assets of 443 billion francs, making it about 10 times smaller than market leader Generale Bank. ($1=32.19 Belgian Franc)
